mainTopic: Houses between courtyards and crossing עירובין (end of הדר), then a window between two courtyards: its size, height, and the measure of a round window
overview: This amud opens with the end of a ruling from the previous daf. Three houses sit between two courtyards: each outer house is a בית שער, and the middle house holds the עירוב. רחבה then tests the רבנן with two houses between two courtyards, where each resident passes through one house and places his עירוב in the other. The רבנן rule that neither עירוב works, because a house cannot be a בית for one person and a בית שער for the other. They also reject רחבה's comparison to רבא's twilight ruling, since a hidden doubt about time is different from a visible house. The chapter הדר ends. A new chapter opens with a משנה about a window between two courtyards: if it is four by four טפחים and within ten טפחים of the ground, the courtyards may share one עירוב. The גמרא shows that even the רבנן agree an opening must be four by four. It also learns that a window only partly within ten still counts, which matches a ברייתא. Finally רבי יוחנן gives the size of a round window, 24 טפחים around, and the גמרא asks why twelve is not enough. The answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Outer houses are gatehouses and the middle house holds the עירוב
steps.stepSummary: This closes the ruling about three houses between two courtyards. Each outer house counts as a בית שער for the courtyard next to it. The middle house is where the עירוב sits, so its residents do not need to contribute bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: This outer house becomes a gatehouse for this courtyard, and that outer house becomes a gatehouse for that courtyard. The middle house is the house in which the עירוב is placed, and its residents do not need to give bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling that began on the previous daf. It explains why some of the residents in a three-house setup do not need to contribute to the עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each outer house is only a passageway for its courtyard, so it is treated as a בית שער, and people living in a בית שער do not contribute to an עירוב. The middle house actually holds the עירוב, and the house that holds the עירוב never needs to give bread. So in this case, labeling each house by its role works out cleanly.

keyTerms.meaning: Gatehouse: an entrance room that serves as a passageway, not a real dwelling, for עירוב purposes
The shared food that joins residents so they may carry on שבת
The middle one (here, the middle house)
Bread, the food each household contributes to the עירוב

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the idea that one house can be labeled by its role (gatehouse, or the house holding the עירוב) relative to a specific courtyard. רחבה's question in the next step pushes exactly on that idea.

phrases.english: this one becomes a gatehouse for this one,
phrases.notes: This outer house serves as the gatehouse of the courtyard it opens to.

phrases.english: and that one becomes a gatehouse for that one.
phrases.notes: The other outer house is the gatehouse of the other courtyard.

phrases.aramaic: אֶמְצָעִי הָוֵה לֵיהּ בַּיִת שֶׁמַּנִּיחִין בּוֹ עֵירוּב,
phrases.english: the middle one is the house in which the eiruv is placed,
and it does not need to give the bread.
phrases.notes: The house holding the עירוב is exempt from contributing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ruling begun on the previous daf (75b).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The outer houses are gatehouses and the middle house is the house holding the עירוב, so none of them needs to contribute bread.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A house between courtyards is labeled by its function: a gatehouse for its courtyard, or the house holding the עירוב.

steps.title: רחבה's test case of two houses with crossing עירובין
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks about two courtyards with two houses between them. Each courtyard's resident walks through the house next to him and places his עירוב in the far house. Can one house be a בית for one courtyard and a בית שער for the other at the same time?
steps.simpleTranslation: רחבה tested the רבנן: Two courtyards with two houses between them. This one came through this house and put his עירוב in that one, and that one came through that house and put his עירוב in this one. Did they acquire the עירוב or not? Do you treat each house as a 'house' for this courtyard and a 'gatehouse' for that one, and the other house as a 'gatehouse' for this one and a 'house' for that one?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה poses a tricky test question to the רבנן. He takes the previous idea, that a house is labeled by its role, and asks whether one house can carry two opposite labels at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the three-house case, each house had a single role. Here each house plays two roles at once: it is the passageway for the courtyard next to it and the house holding the עירוב for the far courtyard. The question is whether we may assign each house a different status depending on which courtyard we are talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: He tested them (asked a question to check their knowledge)
רחבה, an אמורא
They acquired the eiruv (the eiruv took effect for them)
You render them / you treat them as
With respect to, in relation to

steps.confusionAlert: Each resident walks through the house next to him and places his עירוב in the far house, the one next to the other courtyard. That is why each house is a 'house' for one person and a 'gatehouse' for the other.

phrases.english: Rachava tested the Sages:
two courtyards and two houses between them,
this one came by way of this house
phrases.notes: He passed through the house that opens to his own courtyard.

phrases.english: and placed his eiruv in that one,
phrases.notes: He placed it in the farther house.

phrases.english: and that one came by way of that house
and placed his eiruv in this one,
did they acquire the eiruv or not?

phrases.aramaic: מִי מְשַׁוֵּית לְהוּ לְגַבֵּי דְּהַאי בַּיִת,
phrases.english: Do you treat it, with respect to this one, as a house,
and with respect to that one, as a gatehouse
[and the other house, with respect to this one, as a gatehouse,
and with respect to that one, as a house]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the gatehouse/eiruv-house idea to a case where one house has two conflicting roles.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can a single house be a בית for one courtyard and a בית שער for the other at the same time, so that both עירובין work?

steps.title: Neither עירוב works, whichever way you look at it
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן answer that neither resident acquired his עירוב, using a מה נפשך argument. If the house is a בית שער, an עירוב placed there is invalid. If it is a בית, the other person is carrying into a house that is not part of his עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Neither of them acquired the עירוב, whichever way you look at it. If you treat it as a gatehouse, one who puts his עירוב in a gatehouse, porch, or balcony has no valid עירוב. If you treat it as a house, he is carrying into a house that he has not joined in an עירוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן answer רחבה's question. They say both עירובין fail, and they prove it by showing that every possible way of labeling the house leads to a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A house must have one consistent status; you cannot call it a gatehouse for one person and a house for the other. Label it a gatehouse, and the person who placed his עירוב there loses, because an עירוב in a gatehouse is invalid. Label it a house, and the person walking through it loses, because he carries through a dwelling that is not joined to his עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you want (an argument that every option fails)
A porch or portico
A balcony
Carries / moves objects

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן hold that one house cannot have two opposite statuses at once. Since each label harms one of the two people, neither עירוב works.

phrases.english: They said to him:
neither of them acquired the eiruv,
whichever way you want:
if you treat it as a gatehouse,

phrases.aramaic: הַנּוֹתֵן אֶת עֵירוּבוֹ בְּבֵית שַׁעַר אַכְסַדְרָה וּמִרְפֶּסֶת —
phrases.english: one who places his eiruv in a gatehouse, a porch, or a balcony —
phrases.notes: Quoting the established rule from the משנה.

phrases.english: it is not a valid eiruv.
if you treat it as a house —

phrases.aramaic: קָא מְטַלְטֵל לְבַיִת דְּלָא מְעָרֵב לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: he is carrying into a house that he has not joined in an eiruv.
phrases.notes: This refers to the person passing through the house next to his own courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: שְׁנֵיהֶן לֹא קָנוּ עֵירוּב
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Neither acquires the עירוב: the gatehouse label invalidates the placement, and the house label makes the passage forbidden carrying.

steps.title: Challenge from רבא's ruling on twilight עירובין
steps.stepSummary: רחבה challenges the רבנן from a ruling of רבא. Two people each had an עירוב made for them, with בין השמשות treated as day for one and as night for the other. רבא rules that both acquire their עירוב, even though the two assumptions contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how is this different from רבא? For רבא said: Two people told someone, 'Go and make an עירוב for us.' For one he made it while it was still day, and for the other he made it during twilight. The עירוב of the one made by day was eaten during twilight, and the עירוב of the one made at twilight was eaten after nightfall. Both of them acquired the עירוב!
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה pushes back on the רבנן's answer. He points to a ruling of רבא where contradictory assumptions were applied to two people at once, and both still won.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בין השמשות is a doubt: it might be day or night. For the first person, רבא treats it as night, so his עירוב took effect before it was eaten. For the second person, רבא treats it as day, so his עירוב was set up in time. If רבא allows opposite assumptions for two different people, why can't the house be a 'house' for one and a 'gatehouse' for the other?

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the difference? (a challenge formula)
רבא, a leading אמורא
While it is still day
Twilight, a time of doubt between day and night
After it has become dark (nightfall)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא's case is about an עירוב תחומין (שבת limits), not an עירוב חצרות. רחבה is borrowing only its logic: applying contradictory assumptions leniently to two people at once.
steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge sets up the next step, where the גמרא will have to explain why a doubt about time (בין השמשות) can be resolved leniently both ways, while a physical house cannot be given two opposite statuses.

phrases.english: And what is different from Rava's ruling?
For Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ שְׁנַיִם צֵא וְעָרֵב עָלֵינוּ.
phrases.english: Two people said to him: Go and make an eiruv for us.
For one, he made the eiruv while it was still day,
and for the other, he made the eiruv during twilight.
The one for whom he made it while still day —
his eiruv was eaten during twilight,
phrases.notes: Here twilight is treated as night, so the עירוב had already taken effect.

phrases.english: and the one for whom he made it during twilight —
his eiruv was eaten after nightfall —
phrases.notes: Here twilight is treated as day, so the עירוב was set up in time.

phrases.english: both of them acquired the eiruv!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the רבנן's answer by pointing to a parallel case with the opposite outcome.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's claim that one house cannot be treated one way for one person and the opposite way for the other.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא applies contradictory assumptions about בין השמשות to two people at once and validates both עירובין. So contradictory statuses should also be allowed for the house.

steps.title: Why רבא's case is different from the two-house case
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן reject רחבה's comparison. A doubt about בין השמשות cannot be seen, so each person may treat it his own way. A house is a clear physical thing, so it must have the same status for both residents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that a real comparison?! In רבא's case, whether בין השמשות is day or night is a doubt that nobody can see, so the matter is not noticeable. But here, if this place is a 'house' for one person, it is a 'house' for the other person too. And if it is a 'gatehouse' for one, it is also a 'gatehouse' for the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן answer רחבה's challenge. They show that רבא's case is different from the case of two houses between two courtyards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבא's case, nobody knows whether בין השמשות is day or night, and nothing on the ground shows which it is. So we may treat it as day for one person and as night for the other. A house, though, is a visible, physical place with one real function, so it cannot be a בית for one person and a בית שער for the other at the same time. That means the מה נפשך argument from Step 3 stands, and neither resident acquires his עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is that so?! How can you compare?' A phrase that rejects a comparison.
A doubt or uncertainty
The matter is not noticeable or visible
With regard to, in relation to

steps.whatToRemember: A hidden doubt (like בין השמשות) can be ruled differently for different people. A visible physical fact (like the status of a house) must be the same for everyone.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא did not decide that בין השמשות is really both day and night. It stays one unknown, and because nobody can see the answer, each person may rely on a different side of the doubt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a general rule. Contradictory assumptions can sometimes be allowed for a hidden doubt, but not for a visible reality.

phrases.english: Is that so?! (How can you compare?)
There, it is a doubt whether it is day or night
the matter is not noticeable
phrases.notes: Nobody can see which side of the doubt is true.

phrases.english: but here,
if with regard to this one it is a house,
then with regard to that one it is a house.
If with regard to this one it is a gatehouse,
then with regard to that one it is also a gatehouse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 4 by showing that רבא's case is different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (hidden doubt versus visible physical reality)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רחבה thought that, just as רבא allowed contradictory assumptions about בין השמשות, one house could have contradictory statuses for two residents.
steps.terutzMaskana: Contradictory assumptions are allowed only when the doubt cannot be seen. A house's status is visible, so it must be the same for both residents, and neither acquires his עירוב.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter הדר
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the sixth chapter of עירובין, called הדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter הדר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא marks the end of the chapter הדר. This is a closing line, not an argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words הדרן עלך express a wish to come back and learn this chapter again. A new chapter begins right after this line.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you.' The formula said when finishing a chapter.
'One who lives.' The name of this chapter, taken from its first word.

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter 'One who lives'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the final discussion of רחבה's question.

steps.title: A large, low window lets two courtyards choose one עירוב
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules on a window between two courtyards that is four by four טפחים and within ten טפחים of the ground. The courtyards may each make a separate עירוב, or, if they want, they may join together with one עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: מתניתין: A window between two courtyards that is four by four טפחים, and within ten טפחים of the ground: the residents make two עירובין. And if they want, they make one עירוב.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a משנה about a window in the wall between two courtyards. If the window is big enough and low enough, the two courtyards may choose to join as one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A window of four by four טפחים counts as a real opening. Being within ten טפחים of the ground makes it usable for passing things through. Because of that, the two courtyards may act as two separate units or join into one unit, as they prefer.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
A window
Four by four טפחים, the minimum size of a real opening
Within ten טפחים of the ground
They make an עירוב

steps.whyThisMatters: This opening rule sets up the whole chapter. It decides when two areas are connected enough to share one עירוב.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: A window
that is between two courtyards
four by four handbreadths,
within ten handbreadths of the ground —
they make two eruvin.
And if they wish, they make one eruv.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new chapter with a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A window of four by four טפחים within ten טפחים of the ground gives the courtyards a choice: two עירובין, or one shared עירוב.

steps.title: A small or high window means only separate עירובין
steps.stepSummary: If the window is smaller than four by four טפחים, or higher than ten טפחים, it does not connect the courtyards. Each courtyard must make its own עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the window is less than four by four טפחים, or above ten טפחים, they make two עירובין, and they may not make one עירוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the other side of the rule. A window that is too small or too high does not count as a real opening, so the courtyards cannot join.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either flaw on its own removes the choice. If the window is too small, or if it is too high, the wall counts as solid between the courtyards. So the two courtyards stay separate and must make separate עירובין.

keyTerms.meaning: Less than four טפחים
Higher than ten טפחים from the ground
And they may not make one shared עירוב

steps.whatToRemember: To join two courtyards through a window, the window must be at least four by four טפחים and within ten טפחים of the ground. Otherwise, each courtyard makes its own עירוב.

phrases.english: Less than four by four handbreadths
or above ten handbreadths
they make two eruvin,
and they do not make one eruv.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּחוֹת מֵאַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה אוֹ לְמַעְלָה מֵעֲשָׂרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the contrasting case to Step 7: when the window fails the size or height requirement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A window smaller than four by four טפחים, or higher than ten טפחים, does not connect the courtyards. Only separate עירובין are allowed.

steps.title: Does the unattributed משנה follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the משנה's rule (a window smaller than four by four does not count) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds that any gap smaller than four טפחים is treated as closed (לבוד).
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Shall we say that we learned this unattributed משנה according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who said that any gap of less than four טפחים is considered closed, like לבוד?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the new משנה. It suggests that the משנה's four-טפחים measurement matches only one side of a known dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a dispute about לבוד, the rule that a small gap is treated as if it were closed. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says any gap under four טפחים counts as closed, while the רבנן say only a gap under three. Since the משנה treats a window under four as if it were not there, the גמרא suggests the משנה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, which would mean it does not follow the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Shall we say? It introduces a suggestion that may be rejected.
An unattributed (anonymous) teaching
A small gap that halacha treats as closed or joined
תנא who holds that the measure for לבוד is less than four טפחים

steps.confusionAlert: The רבנן also accept the idea of לבוד. They only disagree about its size: they say less than three טפחים, while רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says less than four.

phrases.english: Gemara:
phrases.notes: Marks the start of the גמרא on the new משנה

phrases.english: Shall we say we learned an unattributed teaching
in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
who said: anything less than four handbreadths
phrases.notes: Refers to any gap smaller than four טפחים

phrases.english: is considered as joined (lavud).

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא תְּנַן סְתָמָא כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's analysis of the משנה quoted in steps 7-8
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the משנה's four-by-four requirement follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's measure for לבוד, so that it goes against the רבנן?

steps.title: Even the רבנן agree an opening needs four by four
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. The dispute about לבוד deals only with closing gaps. For something to count as a real opening, everyone agrees it must be four by four.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if you say the משנה follows the רבנן, the רבנן disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל only about לבוד, meaning which gaps count as closed. But about an opening, even the רבנן agree that if it is four by four it is significant, and if not, it is not significant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion. It says the משנה can fit the רבנן as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לבוד asks a different question from the one in our משנה. לבוד asks when a small gap is treated as closed. Our משנה asks when a hole is big enough to count as a real opening. Even the רבנן, who use three טפחים for לבוד, agree that a window must be four by four to be an important opening. So the משנה is not a proof for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say. It shows the משנה can fit the other opinion too.
They only disagree up to this point. It limits the scope of a dispute.
An opening (here, the window)
They agree
It is significant, so it counts

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the size for joining two areas (לבוד) and the size for a meaningful opening are two separate measures. A disagreement about one does not carry over to the other.

phrases.english: Even if you say it follows the Rabbis,
the Rabbis disagree only
with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
regarding the laws of lavud (joining gaps),
but regarding an opening,
even the Rabbis agree

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי אִיכָּא אַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה — חֲשִׁיב,
phrases.english: that if it is four by four, it is significant,
and if not, it is not significant.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole suggestion that the משנה follows only רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It mixes up two different questions: the size of a gap treated as closed (לבוד) and the size of an opening that counts as significant

steps.title: Why state the smaller or higher window case at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's second clause and asks why it was needed. Once the משנה said that four by four within ten joins the courtyards, the opposite case already seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'Less than four, etc.' That is obvious! Since it already said four by four within ten טפחים, I know on my own that less than four, or higher than ten, does not count!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the משנה bothered to state the smaller or higher case, since it seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause of the משנה already sets the conditions: four by four, and within ten טפחים. Anyone can figure out that a window missing these conditions fails to join the courtyards. So the second clause seems to be extra wording, and the גמרא wants to know its purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. This is a challenge that a teaching adds nothing new.
On its own, automatically
Within ten טפחים of the ground
Higher than ten טפחים from the ground

phrases.english: The mishna says: 'Less than four, etc.'
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, step 8

phrases.english: This is obvious!
Since it said four by four
within ten handbreadths,
I already know on my own
that less than four, or above ten, does not count!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the need for the משנה's second clause
steps.kashyaTarget: The second clause of the משנה (step 8)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The clause seems unnecessary because its rule follows directly from the first clause

steps.title: A window only partly within ten still counts
steps.stepSummary: The second clause teaches something new. A window fails to join the courtyards only if all of it is above ten טפחים. If part of it is within ten, the courtyards may still make one עירוב together.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה teaches us: the reason it does not count is that the whole window is above ten. But if part of it is within ten, they make two עירובין, and if they want, they make one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of step 11. It shows that the extra clause teaches a new point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'higher than ten,' which means the entire window is above ten. From this we learn the opposite case: if even part of the window is within ten טפחים, it still counts as a valid opening. In that case the courtyards may choose to join with one עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us. It introduces the new point of a teaching.
The reason, meaning only in this specific case
All of it, the entire window
Part of it

steps.whatToRemember: A window of four by four links two courtyards for עירוב as long as at least part of it is within ten טפחים of the ground. Even the רבנן agree that it must be four by four.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
the reason is that the entire window is above ten,
but if part of it is within ten,
they make two eiruvin,
and if they want, they make one eiruv.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Finding a new point in the wording that seemed extra
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second clause seems to repeat what we already know from the first clause
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause shows that only a window entirely above ten fails. A window partly within ten still joins the courtyards.

steps.title: The משנה's lesson matches a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says that the משנה, as just explained, teaches the same thing as a ברייתא. The ברייתא says that if part of the window is within ten and part is above ten, the courtyards may make two עירובים, or one if they want.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה taught the same thing the רבנן taught in a ברייתא: if nearly all of the window is above ten and a bit is within ten, or nearly all is within ten and a bit is above ten, they make two עירובין, and if they want, they may make one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא remarks that, with this explanation (step 12), our משנה already teaches the same ruling that a ברייתא states explicitly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 12 the גמרא said that a window joins the courtyards unless all of it is above ten. This ברייתא says it outright: if even part of the window is within ten, the courtyards are allowed to make one עירוב together. So the משנה's extra clause and the ברייתא teach the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: We have already learned it (in our משנה)
The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
All of it (here: nearly all of it)
Part of it
They make an עירוב

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'כולו' does not mean the whole window. It means nearly all of it, since the same sentence says that part of it is on the other side of ten.

phrases.english: We have learned in our Mishnah what the Rabbis taught in a baraita:
If nearly all of it is above ten handbreadths
and part of it is within ten,
or nearly all of it is within ten
and part of it is above ten —
they make two separate eiruvin,
and if they wish, they make one eiruv.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 12 by pointing to a matching ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The reading that a window joins the courtyards as long as part of it is within ten.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says that if part of the window is within ten, they may make one עירוב.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא list the easier case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about how the ברייתא is worded. If a window that is mostly above ten (with a bit within ten) already joins the courtyards, it is obvious that a window mostly within ten does too. Why mention it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if nearly all of it is above ten and only a bit is within ten, you said they make two עירובים or one if they want. Is it even a question when nearly all of it is within ten and only a bit is above ten?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for saying something that seems unneeded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The harder case is the window that is mostly too high, and even there the courtyards may join. So the window that is mostly low enough should certainly join them. Listing the easy case after the hard one looks like extra words.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, if (introduces a 'how much more so' argument)
You said
Is it even a question? (it is obvious)

phrases.english: Now, if nearly all of it is above ten
and only part of it is within ten,
you said, "they make two eiruvin
and if they wish, they make one,"
then where nearly all of it is within ten
and only part of it is above ten, is it even necessary to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא כּוּלּוֹ לְמַעְלָה מֵעֲשָׂרָה וּמִקְצָתוֹ בְּתוֹךְ עֲשָׂרָה אָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא brought in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second case listed in the ברייתא (mostly within ten, a bit above).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קל וחומר: if the harder case joins the courtyards, the easier case obviously does, so listing it seems unneeded.

steps.title: A 'this, and certainly that' style
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא uses the style of 'this, and there is no need to say that.' It states the new case and then adds the obvious one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא teaches in the style of 'this, and there is no need to say that.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the extra case is just a teaching style, not a mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא does not mean that the second case is a new idea. It teaches the surprising case first and then mentions the obvious one, as if to say 'and of course this too.' The question goes away because nothing was claimed to be new.

keyTerms.meaning: This, and there is no need to say that (from the harder case to the easier one)
It teaches

steps.whatToRemember: A window joins two courtyards as long as at least part of a four by four opening is within ten טפחים. The ברייתא lists the obvious case only as a 'this, and certainly that' style.

phrases.english: It teaches in the style of "this, and there is no need to say that."

steps.triggerLanguage: זוֹ וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר זוֹ קָתָנֵי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording as a recognized teaching style.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing the easier case seemed like extra, unneeded words.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא teaches the new case and then the obvious one on purpose, in the style 'this, and certainly that.'

steps.title: How big a round window must be
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that a round window must have a circumference of 24 טפחים, with two and a bit of them within ten. That way, a four by four square drawn inside it will have a bit within ten.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: a round window needs a circumference of 24 טפחים, with two and a bit of them within ten, so that if you draw a square inside it, a bit of the square is within ten.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן applies the four by four rule to a round window and gives its needed size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rules so far measure a four by four square, but a round window has no corners. רבי יוחנן says to picture a square drawn inside the circle. The circle must be big enough for that square to be four by four, and low enough that the bottom of the square reaches a bit within ten.

keyTerms.meaning: A round window
Circumference (the distance around)
A tiny bit
He makes it into a square (draws a square inside it)

steps.confusionAlert: The 'two and a bit' are counted from the 24 טפחים around the circle, not as straight height. The circle curves, so the bottom of the square inside sits higher than the bottom of the circle. That is why more than just a sliver of the circle must be within ten.
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns the four by four rule into a working measure for windows that are not square. The גמרא will next question the number 24.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
A round window must have
a circumference of twenty-four handbreadths,
with two and a bit of them within ten handbreadths,
so that if one draws a square inside it,
a bit of the square is found within ten.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: חַלּוֹן עָגוֹל צָרִיךְ שֶׁיְּהֵא בְּהֶיקֵּפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: applying the four by four, within-ten rule to a round window.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A round window must have a 24-טפח circumference, with two and a bit of it within ten, so that a four by four square drawn inside has a bit within ten.

steps.title: Why twenty-four? Twelve should be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן. A circle's circumference is three times its width, so a round window four טפחים wide needs a circumference of only twelve, not twenty-four.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, consider this: any circle whose circumference is three טפחים has a width of one טפח. So twelve טפחים around should be enough!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is attacking רבי יוחנן's number of 24. It uses a basic math rule to argue that half that size, 12, should be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The window must be four טפחים wide. Since the circumference is three times the width, 4 × 3 = 12. רבי יוחנן said 24, which is double, so the גמרא asks why he needs so much.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, consider this. An opening word that brings an accepted fact to start a challenge.
Circumference, the distance around a circle
Width (here, the diameter of the circle)
Twelve
It is enough

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא has proven רבי יוחנן wrong. This is only a question. The answer will show that a four by four square drawn inside a circle needs a bigger circle than a circle only four טפחים wide.

phrases.english: Now, consider:
phrases.notes: This starts a question built on something everyone agrees is true.

phrases.english: anything that has a circumference of three handbreadths
phrases.notes: The standard rule of thumb the גמרא uses for a circle

phrases.english: has a width of one handbreadth.
phrases.notes: So the circumference is three times the width

phrases.english: Twelve should be enough!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדִי, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּהֶיקֵּפוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה טְפָחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the measurement of 24 טפחים given by רבי יוחנן in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that a round window needs a circumference of 24 טפחים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A circumference is three times the width. A window only needs to be four טפחים wide, so a circumference of 12 should be enough. 24 seems far too large.
